summary: Potassium chloride is an electrolyte supplement for treatment and prophylaxis of hypokalemia. This label is the oral extended-release tablet: 40-100 mEq/day in divided doses (max 40 mEq per dose) for treatment and about 20 mEq/day for prevention, taken with meals and a full glass of water, swallowed whole. If serum potassium is below 2.5 mEq/L, use IV potassium instead. CRITICAL safety rule: concentrated potassium chloride injection must always be diluted and never given by IV push/bolus, which is fatal.
indications: Treatment of hypokalemia with or without metabolic alkalosis in patients for whom dietary management or diuretic dose reduction is insufficient
Prophylaxis of hypokalemia with or without metabolic alkalosis in patients for whom dietary management or diuretic dose reduction is insufficient

moa: Potassium is the major intracellular cation, essential for nerve conduction, cardiac and skeletal muscle contraction, acid-base balance, and maintenance of the resting membrane potential. Supplemental potassium chloride replaces potassium and the accompanying chloride lost in hypokalemia, helping correct associated metabolic alkalosis. The chloride salt is preferred because hypokalemia is frequently accompanied by hypochloremic alkalosis.

absolute: Concomitant use with triamterene or amiloride (severe hyperkalemia)
relative: Impaired potassium excretion / significant renal impairment
Dysphagia or GI obstruction/stricture (for solid oral forms)
monitor: Concomitant RAAS inhibitors (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, eplerenone, aliskiren)

preg: There are no human data and no animal reproduction studies. Potassium supplementation that does not produce hyperkalemia is not expected to cause fetal harm, since maternal-fetal potassium is normally regulated.
lact: The normal potassium content of human milk is about 13 mEq/L. As supplemental oral potassium joins the body potassium pool, supplementation has little or no effect on milk potassium levels as long as body potassium is not excessive. Considered compatible with breastfeeding.
renal: Renal impairment markedly increases the risk of dangerous hyperkalemia because potassium excretion is reduced. Initiate therapy at the low end of the dosing range and monitor serum potassium closely; potassium chloride is contraindicated when potassium excretion is severely impaired or hyperkalemia exists.
hepatic: In cirrhosis, an oral potassium load can raise serum potassium roughly twice as much as in normal subjects; initiate therapy at the low end of the dosing range and monitor.

major: Triamterene or amiloride - severe hyperkalemia; concomitant use is contraindicated
moderate: RAAS inhibitors (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, eplerenone, aliskiren) - potassium retention; closely monitor potassium
NSAIDs - reduce potassium excretion; closely monitor potassium
Digitalis - rapid potassium shifts can affect digitalis effect/toxicity

interactions.food: Take with meals and a full glass of water; large intake of potassium-rich foods or salt substitutes adds to potassium load.
interactions.diagnostics: Raises serum potassium; monitor ECG for peaked T-waves, loss of P-wave, ST depression and QT prolongation that signal hyperkalemia.

missed: Take the missed dose with food and water when remembered, unless it is almost time for the next dose; then skip it and resume the regular schedule. Do not double up.
overdose: Oral overdose rarely causes serious hyperkalemia when potassium excretion is normal, but impaired excretion can produce fatal hyperkalemia. Hyperkalemia is often asymptomatic until ECG changes (peaked T-waves, lost P-wave, ST depression, QT prolongation) and late muscle paralysis or cardiac arrest (9-12 mEq/L). Treatment: stop all potassium sources and potassium-sparing agents; give IV dextrose with insulin, correct acidosis with sodium bicarbonate, and use exchange resins or dialysis. Beware delayed absorption from extended-release tablets; in digitalized patients lower potassium gradually to avoid digitalis toxicity.
